Historical Background
Date & Era

1066 CE · Medieval England · End of Anglo-Saxon rule and the Norman Conquest
A disputed succession brought Harold II and William of Normandy into a struggle for the English crown.

The Opposing Armies

King Harold II defended the ridge with household warriors and levies fighting on foot. Duke William brought Norman, Breton and other contingents, combining archers, infantry and cavalry.

Why They Fought

Edward the Confessor died in 1066 without a direct heir. English nobles chose Harold, while William claimed that the succession had been promised to him and assembled an invasion fleet. Harold defeated a Norwegian invasion in the north, then marched south to face the Normans.

The Battle

On 14 October the English held the heights with shields and spears, while elite warriors fought with axes. Norman archers, infantry and cavalry attacked repeatedly. Some English troops pursued retreating enemies away from their formation and high ground, exposing themselves to counterattack. Fighting continued into the evening.

Historical Outcome

Harold was killed and the English line collapsed. William later entered London and was crowned king. Harold’s precise manner of death and some tactical details remain disputed. Formation discipline and the combined protection of spears, shields and terrain are central to the battle.

Recommended Side · English Army

Tactics
Hold four spear companies facing west in front of the north and south flags. Use Hold (X) to brace; moving or pursuing lowers their spears.
Shields absorb arrows. Keep axemen behind the spear line and archers on the reverse slope. Turn nearby pikes to meet cavalry on the flanks.
Secure one flag first. Avoid chasing cavalry downhill with the entire army; select individual companies and leave a reserve at the other flag.

Victory Conditions
English: hold at least one ridge flag for nine minutes, or rout the Normans.

Historical Background
Date & Era

1297 CE · Medieval Scotland · First War of Scottish Independence
Scottish resistance challenged English occupation at the strategically important crossing of the Forth.

The Opposing Armies

William Wallace and Andrew Moray jointly led the Scots. The English army under John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, and Hugh de Cressingham sought to restore English control of Scotland.

Why They Fought

Edward I invaded Scotland in 1296, forced King John Balliol to submit and installed English administration and garrisons. Resistance spread the following year. Wallace and Moray joined forces as an English army advanced north; Stirling controlled a vital route across the Forth.

The Battle

On 11 September 1297 the English crossed a narrow wooden bridge. The Scots waited on the far-side heights until part of the army was across but the rest remained constrained by the bridge. Their attack isolated the vanguard, denied room to deploy and obstructed its escape.

Historical Outcome

The crossing force suffered a heavy defeat. Cressingham died and Surrey withdrew; Moray later died of his wounds. The victory strengthened Scottish resistance. Today’s stone bridge is later than the battle, and the precise position of the original bridge and fighting remains uncertain.

Historical Background
Date & Era

219 CE · Late Eastern Han · Struggle for Hanzhong
Liu Bei and Cao Cao contested the mountain approaches between the Guanzhong region and Yi Province.

The Opposing Armies

Liu Bei commanded the attacking army, with Huang Zhong leading the assault and Fa Zheng advising. Xiahou Yuan, Zhang He and other officers defended Hanzhong for Cao Cao. Shu Han had not yet been founded.

Why They Fought

Cao Cao’s possession of Hanzhong threatened Liu Bei’s northern approaches in Yi Province. Taking it would provide both a defensive barrier and a route north. The armies therefore fought for mountain positions and fortified camps.

The Battle

In 219 Liu Bei crossed south of Yangping over the Mian River and established positions near Mount Dingjun. Xiahou Yuan contested the ground. Huang Zhong seized an opportunity to attack from above, breaking the defenders and killing Xiahou Yuan. Different biographies emphasize different camp attacks and troop movements.

Historical Outcome

Zhang He helped restore order. Cao Cao later arrived with another army but eventually withdrew. Liu Bei secured Hanzhong and strengthened Yi Province’s northern defenses. High ground, camps and the timing of the assault explain the battle’s importance.

Historical Background
Date & Era

1415 CE · Medieval England and France · Hundred Years’ War
Henry V’s exhausted army, marching toward Calais, faced a larger French force blocking its route.

The Opposing Armies

Henry V led English longbowmen and men-at-arms. French nobles under Constable Charles d’Albret commanded a force with many armored men-at-arms. The main French assault was not conducted entirely on horseback.

Why They Fought

Claims to the French crown and disputed territories underlay the Hundred Years’ War. Henry invaded in 1415 and captured Harfleur, but disease and campaigning weakened his army. He marched toward English-held Calais as the French moved to intercept him.

The Battle

On 25 October the English took a narrow position between woods, with stakes protecting the archers. Rain-soaked ground slowed the French. Arrow fire disrupted their advance, while dense armored formations and following troops compressed those fighting at the front.

Historical Outcome

The English won, and many French nobles were killed or captured. Henry’s political standing rose. Army-size estimates vary considerably. The battle resulted from the interaction of shooting, obstacles, mud and a restricted frontage.

Historical Background
Date & Era

216 BCE · Roman Republic · Second Punic War
Rome sought a decisive victory over Hannibal, whose invasion and seizure of supplies threatened Italy.

The Opposing Armies

Hannibal commanded African, Iberian and Gallic infantry with several cavalry contingents. Roman and allied troops were led by both consuls, Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro; responsibility cannot be assigned to Varro alone.

Why They Fought

During the Second Punic War Hannibal crossed the Alps and defeated successive Roman armies. Rome raised a larger force to destroy him in a pitched battle. His seizure of the supply center at Cannae added pressure to seek a decision.

The Battle

In 216 BCE deep Roman infantry formations pressed into the center. Hannibal’s forward center gradually yielded into a concave line. African infantry on the wings turned inward, while victorious cavalry struck the Roman rear, completing an encirclement.

Historical Outcome

Roman losses were catastrophic. Paullus died and Varro escaped, but Rome continued the war. Cannae shows how a dense center can lose the ability to deploy or withdraw when its flanks and rear collapse.

Historical Background

341 BCE · Warring States · Rivalry between Qi and Wei
Qi intervened after Wei attacked Han, drawing Wei’s troops back toward their own territory.

The Opposing Armies

Tian Ji commanded Qi’s army with Sun Bin directing its plans. Pang Juan led Wei’s pursuit; Crown Prince Shen also participated. Han’s request for relief was the immediate background to the campaign.

Why They Fought

Wei attacked Han, which sought Qi’s aid. Rather than meet the main army in Han, Qi threatened Wei’s heartland and drew its army back. Sun Bin then exploited Wei’s contempt for Qi’s troops to prepare an ambush.

The Battle

The Records of the Grand Historian describes Qi reducing its cooking fires each day to suggest desertion. Pang Juan left the infantry behind and pursued with picked troops. Entering the narrow Maling road at night, the vanguard was struck by coordinated crossbow fire triggered by a light.

Historical Outcome

Wei suffered a severe defeat. Pang Juan died and Crown Prince Shen was captured, raising Qi’s standing. The inscribed-tree episode comes from transmitted historical accounts; its details cannot all be tied to precisely identified archaeological locations.

Historical Background
Date & Era

204 BCE · End of Qin and early Han · Chu–Han Contention
Han Xin expanded east across the Taihang Mountains to seize Zhao territory during the Chu–Han struggle.

The Opposing Armies

Han Xin and Zhang Er led the Han force against King Xie of Zhao and Chen Yu. The battle formed part of Han’s eastward expansion during the Chu–Han Contention.

Why They Fought

After defeating Wei and Dai, Han Xin advanced toward Zhao to gain northern manpower and secure Han’s flank. Zhao held the Jingxing exit. Li Zuoche advised avoiding a frontal decision and cutting Han’s supplies, but Chen Yu rejected the proposal.

The Battle

Zhao’s army panicked after losing its camp. Chen Yu was killed and King Xie captured. The riverbank formation fixed the enemy; reconnaissance, deception and the separate camp attack were equally important. Victory was not simply the result of having no retreat.
